body.p: Claims 1-58 are pending in this application. Claims 1-58 now stand rejected.
New claims 59-62 are presented for examination.
Claims 1-58 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to an abstract idea without significantly more.

Applicant respectfully traverses the present rejection for the following reasons. Independent claims 1 and 51 are amended such that the artificially-created data is processed by a trained recurrent neural network model by a method that includes a step of "(f) modifying one or more parameters of simulated animal data to alter physiological, biomechanical, or environmental conditions for predictive analysis." The step of modifying one or more parameters of simulated animal data to alter physiological, biomechanical, or environmental conditions for predictive analysis when combined with steps a) to e) presents a solution to a technical problem by enabling a dynamically adaptable predictive model that goes beyond conventional data analysis. Traditional physiological monitoring systems rely on static data sets or historical trends, which limit their ability to forecast conditions under unobserved scenarios. The claimed invention addresses this limitation by allowing the modification of simulated animal data, ensuring that predictive models can account for changing physiological states, environmental influences, and biomechanical variations. This capability is not merely data processing, but an active computational transformation that enables improved fatigue prediction, injury prevention, and performance optimization. By incorporating real-time parameter adjustments, the claimed method creates a feedback loop within the predictive model, making it responsive to new or hypothetical conditions that were not part of the original dataset. This step improves the reliability and accuracy of AI- driven physiological forecasting, making it a technical advancement over conventional static modeling techniques that fail to generalize beyond predefined conditions.

Unlike conventional data processing techniques, the claims train an RNN model using timestamped, event-based physiological data, incorporating multi-epoch training, an error metric, and an optimizer for updating network weights, which directly enhances the accuracy of predicting fatigue-related events. The invention is not merely using AI for data classification but is actively generating and modifying simulated data through in-sample and out-of-sample forecasting, allowing the model to predict future physiological values based on previously unseen data. For example, the dynamic simulation of fatigue indicators, including heart rate, diastolic blood pressure, systolic blood pressure, perspiration rate, and distance run, is not simply a passive computation but a fundamental improvement to predictive analytics that provides practical applications in sports performance monitoring and real-time physiological assessment. The modification of simulated animal data to alter physiological, biomechanical, or environmental conditions ensures that the generated data is not merely a derivative of collected real-world data but a transformed dataset tailored for predictive analysis, demonstrating a concrete real-world application beyond mere data collection and analysis.

The system claim further confirms that the invention is not an abstract idea but a practical application of machine learning in a structured data-processing environment. The claimed system integrates one or more sensors, including a biological sensor, into a computing device that executes

a trained RNN model to generate and assess simulated data for fatigue analysis. By specifying that at least a portion of the artificially-created data is processed through a trained recurrent neural network, the claim ensures that the model does not merely perform generic AI tasks but applies a specifically trained neural network to physiological data in a structured and meaningful way. The use of in-sample and out-of-sample forecasting further distinguishes the claim from generic AI applications by ensuring that the model can predict physiological conditions beyond previously collected data, directly enhancing real-world accuracy and usability.

The claimed invention is not a fundamental economic or mathematical principle but rather a machine-learning-based system that enhances physiological monitoring by transforming and predicting fatigue-related biometric data. Because the claims do not merely recite a mental process, mathematical calculation, or conventional data gathering, but instead apply an advanced neural network model in a structured and specific manner, they are not directed to an abstract idea and instead integrate AI into a practical application with clear technical benefits. The claims, therefore, satisfy both steps of the Alice test, as they are directed to a specific, technical improvement in physiological data modeling and predictive fatigue analysis and include elements that amount to significantly more than any potential abstract idea. Therefore, the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101 should be withdrawn.

The newly added claims 59-62 further enhance patentability under 35 U.S.C. § 101 by demonstrating practical applications and specific technical improvements that move beyond mere data collection or analysis. Claim 59 strengthens the patent eligibility argument by specifying that the predicted fatigue levels or expected caloric expenditure are delivered as actionable outputs, ensuring that the method is not directed to an abstract idea but to a real-world decision-making system with tangible benefits in athletic monitoring. Claim 60 explicitly defines how modifying simulated animal data alters key physiological conditions, making the claimed invention a dynamic predictive system rather than a static computational model. By specifically adjusting factors such as heart rate and hydration, the claim clarifies that the modification step simulates real-world conditions in a way conventional models do not, reinforcing that the method is not merely abstract but provides a concrete technological solution.

New claim 61 further solidifies patentability by emphasizing real-time or near real-time recalibration of predictive models, demonstrating that the method actively adapts and refines fatigue predictions as an athletic event progresses. This real-time adjustment capability highlights a significant technical improvement over conventional regression-based models, ensuring that the system continuously integrates new data and updates predictions dynamically rather than operating on historical data alone. Finally, claim 62 enhances the eligibility of the invention by explicitly incorporating forecasting of future biological readings, demonstrating that the system is not limited to past or present conditions but predicts future physiological states, a critical distinction from prior conventional monitoring techniques. These claims collectively reinforce that the invention is not an abstract mathematical model but a technological innovation that enhances predictive accuracy and real-time decision-making in athletic event monitoring.
Accordingly, claims 1-58 and new claims 59-62 are now allowable under 35 U.S.C. 101.

Applicant has made a genuine effort to respond to each of the Examiner's objections and rejections in advancing the prosecution of this case. Applicant believes that all formal and substantive requirements for patentability have been met and that this case is in condition for allowance, which action is respectfully requested.
